section_summary: This section opens with a comprehensive State Department docket list of papers (sub-numbers 886 through 1174) recording documents on Japanese political affairs from 1940 to 1943. It is followed by primary diplomatic telegrams from early 1940 and September 1940 detailing the collapse of the Abe Cabinet, the formation of the Yonai and Konoye Cabinets, and inside reports on Japanese political dynamics. Key topics include the pervasive influence of the military over civilian government, debates over moderate versus extremist factions, and allied diplomatic maneuvers regarding U.S.-Japanese and Soviet-Japanese relations.

subfiles.about: A comprehensive Department of State docket register listing incoming and outgoing correspondence, intelligence reports, and memoranda on Japanese political affairs covering sub-numbers 886 through 1174.
subfiles.summary: This multi-page docket list catalogs diplomatic papers filed under decimal file 894.00 between January 1940 and early 1943. The entries record telegrams, despatches, and memoranda documenting major political developments in Japan, including the resignations and appointments of the Abe, Yonai, Konoye, and Tojo cabinets. It also indexes reports on the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, the New Structure movement, Tripartite Pact negotiations, relations with the Soviet Union, and escalating tensions with the United States.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Political Affairs - Japan (File 894.00, Sub-numbers 886-1174)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits a memorandum by Minister John C. Wiley detailing a frank conversation with Japanese diplomat 'Mr. Y.' regarding internal political instability and foreign policy under the Konoye regime.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a strictly confidential report by Minister John C. Wiley recounting an interview with prominent Japanese diplomat 'Mr. Y.', who asserted that the new Konoye administration would not last long and described claimed national unity as a fiction. The informant stated that the recall of diplomats abroad was the regime's sole significant policy act, and predicted that recalled envoys would resume active duties once the government fell. He further reported that alignment with the Axis remained unconsummated, that General Tatekawa was departing for Moscow, and that prospective appointees were refusing the difficult ambassadorial post in Washington. A corrected copy of section two of the telegram is attached.
subfiles.title: Telegram 806 from Tokyo (Grew) transmitting Memorandum of Conversation with Japanese Diplomat

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew discloses the identity of confidential informant 'Mr. Y.' cited in telegram 806 as former Ambassador to Poland Kazu Sakoh.
subfiles.summary: Grew identifies informant 'Mr. Y.' of telegram 806 as Kazu Sakoh, formerly Japanese Ambassador to Poland.
subfiles.title: Telegram 807 from Tokyo (Grew) identifying Informant 'Mr. Y.' as Kazu Sakoh

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on political conferences held by Premier Abe during the holidays and press anticipation of Cabinet decisions on China policy.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Premier Abe's holiday conferences; the Asahi expects a January 4 cabinet meeting on a new central China regime and party relations.
subfiles.title: Telegram 1 from Tokyo (Grew) on Premier Abe's Political Conferences and Cabinet Outlook

subfiles.about: The Department of State refers the Embassy in Tokyo to enclosures in mail instruction 812 of July 27, 1935, in partial reference to Tokyo's telegram 4.
subfiles.summary: Department telegram recalls the enclosures to its Instruction No. 812 of July 27, 1935, in further reference to Tokyo's telegram No. 4.
subfiles.title: Telegram 14 to Tokyo regarding Department Instruction 812 of 1935

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits and analyzes a detailed telegram from British Ambassador Craigie evaluating Japanese political factions, moderate versus extremist forces, and recommended Allied policy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew conveys a extensive paraphrase of a message sent to London by British Ambassador Sir Robert Craigie commenting on views reported by Lord Lothian regarding U.S. policy toward Japan. Craigie argues that a real distinction exists between Japanese moderates seeking economic expansion and extremists aiming for world domination, warning that excessive American economic pressure could push Japan into an extremist dictatorship aligned with the Soviet Union. He urges the British and American governments to moderate economic pressure and offer economic compensation outside China to encourage benevolent Japanese neutrality in the European war. Grew notes his substantial agreement with Craigie's views and emphasizes that while the Japanese army cannot be excluded from power, diplomacy should encourage moderate statesmanship along the lines of Baron Shidehara.
subfiles.title: Telegram 4 from Tokyo (Grew) transmitting British Ambassador Craigie's Views on Japan

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Hull clarifies and corrects British Ambassador Craigie's characterization of informal State Department conversations with Lord Lothian.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Craigie's report of talks with Lord Lothian distorted informal American views: the comparison was between governing groups, and a southward drive was unlikely while Japan was bogged down in China.
subfiles.title: Telegram 9 to Tokyo commenting on Craigie's Report of Discussions with Lord Lothian

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the unfolding political crisis surrounding the Abe Cabinet and conditions set by General Ugaki for forming a new government.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Abe Cabinet will resign soon. Ugaki was approached, demanding a free hand to negotiate with the US; Terauchi and Sato or Matsuoka contemplated, Hata the alternative.
subfiles.title: Telegram 12 from Tokyo (Grew) on Cabinet Crisis and Negotiations with General Ugaki

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reviews public speculation regarding Prince Konoye and other candidates to succeed Premier Abe, noting the crucial impact of relations with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the press favors Konoye to succeed Abe, though reluctant; others mentioned. Press links the crisis to worsening US commercial relations and raw materials.
subfiles.title: Telegram 17 from Tokyo (Grew) on Candidates to Succeed Premier Abe and U.S.-Japan Relations

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the resignation of Premier Abe and the Emperor's directive to Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Yuasa to recommend a successor.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Abe's cabinet resigned and the Emperor told Yuasa to recommend a successor. Konoye refuses and the army avoids responsibility, prolonging selection.
subfiles.title: Telegram 18 from Tokyo (Grew) on Resignation of Abe Cabinet and Selection of New Premier

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports that Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai has received the Imperial Command to form a new Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai received the Imperial Command to form a new Cabinet after Abe's resignation.
subfiles.title: Telegram 19 from Tokyo (Grew) on Imperial Command to Admiral Yonai to Form Cabinet
